body:
> Found while clearing the todo and review lanes on 2026-09-02. Two worktrees for finished cards have been un-reclaimable for hours, and the dispatch log has skipped them on every tick since.

## What happens

`removeWorktree` (`src/gc.js`) reads the pid out of the worktree lock and treats `pidAlive(pid)` as proof the session still owns the checkout:

```js
if (w.locked) {
  const pm = /pid (\d+)/.exec(w.locked);
  if (pm && pidAlive(Number(pm[1]))) return { result: 'locked', pid: Number(pm[1]) };
  git(root, ['worktree', 'unlock', w.path]);
}
```

Claude Code does not exit a finished worker's process. It **recycles it into a background spare pool**, so the pid stays alive indefinitely under a new job:

```
pid 195775: claude bg-spare --bg-spare /tmp/cc-daemon-1000/d25c3cd9/spare/d72abef4.claim.sock
pid 463367: claude bg-spare --bg-spare /tmp/cc-daemon-1000/d25c3cd9/spare/ea438784.claim.sock
```

The lock says `claude session kb-191-1 (pid 195775 start 1098055)`. The session is long over; the process is not. So the lock is never released and the worktree is never removed — on any tick, ever.

## What it is not

**Not pid reuse.** The lock records the process start jiffies, and they still match `/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22 exactly for both. This really is the same process that took the lock; it simply outlived the role it took it for. A start-time check — the obvious first idea, and the one the lock string is already shaped for — would not catch this.

## Observed

- `.claude/worktrees/kb-191-1` on `kb/191-root`, and `.claude/worktrees/kb-217-1` on `kb/217`.
- Both cards closed completed; both PRs (#236, #271) merged. Nothing is stranded — `git cherry origin/main kb/191-root` is 0, and #271's symbols are on main. The three-dot diffs are the usual squash artifact, not unlanded work.
- 9 skip lines in the current `.kanban/logs/dispatch.log`, one per gc pass, growing.

## The shape of the fix

#205 already built this vocabulary for the dispatcher's own pid claim: `cmdlineIsOurs` corroborates a timestamp verdict against `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`, under the rule that **corroboration only rescues, never manufactures**. The same corroboration belongs here — a live pid whose command line is no longer that worker's session is not a reason to keep a lock.

## Done when

- `removeWorktree` frees a worktree whose lock names a live pid whose `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` is not that worker's session, and the log line says why it overrode the lock rather than going silent.
- A pid that genuinely still is the worker keeps its lock. This must never remove a running worker's checkout, and a test asserts that with a live pid whose cmdline does match.
- Where the cmdline cannot be read at all (macOS, a restricted /proc), behaviour is exactly today's: keep the lock, skip quietly. Absence of corroboration is never evidence.
- A test covers the three states through the existing gc double: matching cmdline (keep), non-matching cmdline (reclaim), unreadable (keep).
- The two worktrees above are gone after a `hkb gc --yes` on this checkout.
goal: gc reclaims a worktree whose lock names a live pid that is no longer that worker, corroborated by cmdline the way pidClaimStale does, never touching a genuine live worker and never acting where /proc cannot be read
title: A finished worker's process is recycled into a spare pool, so its worktree lock never expires and gc can never reclaim the checkout
